pullRequest.body: ## Summary - add the 24-package MDFN authoring platform, with framework-neutral core, Markdown/source/render layers, extensions, collaboration, persistence, and framework adapters - add complete React, Svelte, and Solid example applications with desktop and mobile browser workflows - close the SFN-20 audit and re-audit findings across preservation, security, synchronization, accessibility, package boundaries, and server behavior - integrate MDFN editing paths with ContentFn server and CmsFn Studio, and enforce the package graph from the root verification workflow ## Verification - `npm run verify:mdfn` - 24 package builds, type checks, tests, and pack checks - clean React, Svelte, and Solid consumer production/SSR checks - 12 example-app browser runs across Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, and mobile Chromium - `npm run typecheck --prefix contentfn/server` - `npm test --prefix contentfn/server` — 112 tests passed - `npm run typecheck --prefix cmsfn/studio` - `npm test --prefix cmsfn/studio` — 51 tests passed ## Scope notes - MDFN `.conduct` artifacts are included because this PR targets `next` - no `.gitignore` change was needed; existing `dist/` and `test-results/` rules cover generated outputs Linear: https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-20/build-mdfn-as-the-superfunctions-markdown-authoring-platform --- ## Summary by cubic Builds and integrates the MDFN Markdown authoring platform across ContentFn, CmsFn Studio, and DocsFn, delivering SFN-20. Previously Markdown was handled as `richtext` or raw strings; now schemas declare `kind: "markdown"` fields that render with MDFN in Studio, validate and persist profile-bound Markdown on the server, and render via MDFN with stricter URL/HTML policy in DocsFn. - Adds 24 `mdfn/*` packages (core, markdown, render, extensions, framework components, collab, client, contentfn bridge, adapter-kit) and their tests. - `@contentfn/core`: introduces `kind: "markdown"` field with `dialect`, `allowRawHtml`, `extensions`, `schemaVersion`; adds validation and tests. - `cmsfn/studio`: adds `MarkdownWidget` and routes `markdown` fields to the MDFN React editor shell; updates aliases and tests. - `@contentfn/server`: migrates legacy string Markdown to a versioned profile-bound `text/markdown` value, parses with `@mdfn/markdown` and `@mdfn/extensions`, persists profile/sidecar; tightens patch error typing; adds tests. - `docsfn/core`: compiles via `@mdfn/markdown`/`@mdfn/render`, projects MDFN diagnostics, and blocks unsafe URLs by default; adds dependencies and Node engine guard. - Test configs add source aliases for local builds; `engines` raised to Node 20 in `cmsfn/studio`, `@contentfn/server`, and `docsfn/core`. **Migration and rollout** - Upgrade Node to >=20 for affected packages. - Update schemas to use `{ kind: "markdown", dialect?: "commonmark" | "gfm", allowRawHtml?, extensions?, schemaVersion? }` for Markdown fields; Studio will render the MDFN editor automatically. - Expect DocsFn to block unsafe links and emit diagnostics; adjust content or host sanitizer/allowlist if needed. - Existing string Markdown values continue to work; the server migrates them to the profile-bound format on write. Written for commit 55bee8e4126d1e631e827d140a861a1e37e9aae9. Summary will update on new commits.

SFN-20 Build mdfn as the Superfunctions Markdown authoring platform

## Executive summary Create **mdfn**, a framework-neutral Markdown authoring platform for the Superfunctions ecosystem. The product should combine a headless editing engine, first-class Markdown parsing and serialization, a vanilla DOM surface, equal framework adapters, composable editor UI built with UIFn, and optional self-hosted collaboration and platform integrations. The durable contract is Markdown source. Runtime editor state may use a structured document model, but import, editing, export, migrations, diagnostics, and extension behavior must preserve source meaning and avoid silently discarding unsupported content. ## Problem / opportunity Superfunctions has useful pieces for Markdown rendering, portable content blocks, file handling, search, UI, authentication, HTTP, and database access, but it does not yet have a shared authoring substrate. Existing Markdown compilation is renderer-oriented, and existing rich-text authoring surfaces do not provide a complete editing engine. Without mdfn, each product must independently solve schema design, selection behavior, commands, history, clipboard handling, source mode, framework integration, UI parity, persistence, collaboration, and security. A shared Markdown-native platform can remove that duplication while improving interoperability across DocsFn, ContentFn, CmsFn, FileFn, SearchFn, AuthFn, and the shared HTTP/database packages. ## Expected outcome A production-ready, self-hostable Markdown platform that supports: * Headless document and command APIs independent of UI framework * Canonical Markdown parsing, serialization, formatting, and diagnostics * Visual, source, split, preview, and read-only modes * Vanilla DOM integration plus semantically equivalent React, Svelte, and Solid adapters * UIFn-based editor chrome without coupling editing semantics to UIFn * Extensible schema, syntax, commands, keymaps, paste/input rules, rendering, migrations, and tests * Optional collaboration, presence, comments, suggestions, history, assets, persistence, and AI integration * Reuse by DocsFn, ContentFn, CmsFn, FileFn, and SearchFn through explicit compatibility contracts ## Goals * Define the source-preservation contract before implementation. * Support byte-identical no-edit import/export, semantic round trips for supported syntax, and touched-region normalization. * Establish CommonMark as the baseline and GFM as the default dialect. * Preserve unsupported constructs as diagnosable opaque nodes rather than silently dropping them. * Provide a small stable package graph with explicit dependency directions. * Keep the core framework-neutral, UI-neutral, storage-neutral, transport-neutral, and collaboration-neutral. * Provide equal behavior across vanilla DOM, React, Svelte, and Solid. * Use shared Superfunctions abstractions for HTTP, database, authentication, files, search, and UI. * Ship conformance, parity, security, accessibility, browser, IME, clipboard, SSR, performance, migration, and packed-consumer test gates. ## Non-goals * Building browser editing primitives, history, clipboard semantics, or collaborative merge algorithms from scratch. * Coupling the core document model to a UI framework or component library. * Replacing DocsFn, ContentFn, CmsFn, FileFn, SearchFn, AuthFn, or shared packages. * Making executable mixed-framework syntax part of the default portable Markdown dialect. * Enabling raw HTML by default. * Creating one workspace package per document node or mark. * Shipping implementation as part of this backlog-capture item. ## Acceptance criteria * A reviewed product and architecture contract defines the durable Markdown model, runtime document model, source spans, syntax metadata, opaque-node behavior, diagnostics, migrations, and versioning. * The package dependency graph and public/private package boundaries are explicit and mechanically enforceable. * The extension SDK contract covers schema, parsing, serialization, HTML rendering and sanitization, commands, shortcuts, input and paste rules, plugins, migrations, DOM renderers, and conformance tests. * A framework contract defines vanilla DOM behavior and adapter parity requirements for React, Svelte, and Solid. * An editor capability matrix covers foundational editing, Markdown-native syntax, assets and embeds, UI surfaces, collaboration, persistence, import/export, and read-only rendering. * Ecosystem integration contracts are defined for UIFn, DocsFn, ContentFn, CmsFn, FileFn, SearchFn, AuthFn, and shared HTTP/database packages. * Security defaults and threat models cover raw HTML, links, pasted HTML, custom embeds, asset access, collaboration authorization, and denial-of-service inputs. * Release gates cover parser and serializer conformance, round trips, unknown syntax, framework parity, browsers, mobile, IME, clipboard, SSR, accessibility, security, fuzzing, performance, packaging, migrations, and ecosystem adoption. * The work is decomposed into independently verifiable delivery phases with explicit exit criteria. * The two associated Linear documents remain the canonical rationale and delivery-plan references for this issue. ## Dependencies / risks * The source-preservation guarantee constrains parser, runtime model, serializer, migrations, and collaboration design; postponing it risks irreversible architecture mistakes. * A structured editing kernel and collaboration engine must be selected through focused risk spikes and license, bundle, SSR, browser, mobile, and IME evaluation. * Framework adapters can drift unless all behavior is implemented in shared core and adapter layers and verified through the same semantic trace suite. * UIFn package-boundary enforcement must be reliable before mdfn adopts the same graph-verification pattern. * DocsFn adoption requires a compatibility projection so existing rendering behavior can migrate without a flag day. * ContentFn and CmsFn need explicit Markdown content types and migration paths rather than silent reinterpretation of current rich-text data. * Collaboration, comments, and suggestions require stable identifiers, schema-aware migrations, authorization hooks, auditability, and offline conflict handling. * Untrusted Markdown, HTML, links, embeds, assets, and pasted content create security and resource-exhaustion risks. * Package surface area can grow rapidly; stable packages must remain few, with optional capabilities and subpath exports used deliberately. ## Open questions * Which source-preservation level is mandatory for the first stable release, and which syntax classes may normalize? * Which structured editing kernel best satisfies the framework, browser, SSR, IME, bundle, licensing, and plugin requirements? * Which syntax belongs in the default dialect versus opt-in extension packs? * What is the stable public boundary between mdfn parsing/rendering and DocsFn-specific behavior? * Should collaboration and persistence ship in the first stable platform release or follow the headless/browser foundation? * Which content migrations are required for existing ContentFn and CmsFn data? * What are the initial performance budgets for document size, parse latency, keystroke latency, memory, and collaboration fan-out? * Which capabilities belong in the facade package versus explicit advanced imports? ##
